lawyer:
MA Aziz Khan, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 

No one—For the Respondents.
parties:
Mojibur Rahman @ Babu ------ Petitioner
vs
Deputy Commissioner, Kushtia and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Tariq-ul Hakim J : Rule Nisi was issued under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 27-4-1998 (Annexure J) passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court Special Tribunal No. 3, Kushtia in Special Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997 arising out of GR No. 119 of 1996 corresponding to Mirpur PSC Case No. 6(11)96 against the petitioner should not be declared as arbitrary, illegal and without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Facts relevant for the disposed of the Rule is that the petitioner Mojibur Rahman @ Babu while under interrogation on remand in connection with Mirpur PS Case No.6 dated 15-8-1996 made a confession to the police that he was in possession of a shutter gun and ammunition for his personal safety which he kept under the mattress of his bed in the bed room of his house at Swroupdah. The Investigating Officer of the said case after recording necessary GD Entry at Mirpur Police Station proceeded with his force to the petitioner's homestead at Swroupdah to verify his statement and on reaching the same the petitioner from beneath the mattress of his bed brought out in the presence of witnesses a shutter gun about 25 inches long capable of firing rifle cartridges and one round 303 rifle cartridge in a plastic bag. Thereafter, the informant filed an ejahar with Mirpur Police Station against the petitioner under sections 19A and (f) of the Arms Act on the basis of which a regular criminal case was started against him. Thereafter, on 21-12-1996 charge-sheet under sections 19A and (f) of the Arms Act read with section 26 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 was submitted against the petitioner in the aforesaid case and ultimately, the case record ended up in the Court of the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court and Special Tribunal No. 3, Kushtia for trial as Special Tribunal Case No.2 of 1997. 

 3. On perusal of the order sheet of the said case it appears that charge was framed in presence of the petitioner on 6-4-1997 and thereafter he was granted bail by the said tribunal on 5-5-1997. PWs 1 and 2 were examined in presence of the petitioner by the said tribunal on 25-5-1997. Despite being on bail the petitioner did not attend the Court on the subsequent dates fixed by the Special Tribunal although he took steps through his lawyer for filing petition for his absence on 9-10-1997 but the learned Special Tribunal cancelled his bail on the next date i.e. on 26-1-1998 and ordered issuance of warrant of arrest. On 19-3-1998, the petitioner was also absent and PWs 3, 4 and 5 were examined by the Special Tribunal. The petitioner continued to be absent in the subsequent date fixed by the tribunal on 21-4-98 as well and, as such, he could not be examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 27-4-1998 the learned Special Tribunal delivered judgment in the aforesaid special tribunal case and found the petitioner guilty of the offence charged and sentenced him to suffer 14 years rigorous imprisonment and to pay a fine of Taka 5,000 in default to suffer 6 months more. Although the petitioner was not present in court at the time of delivery of judgment he was nevertheless brought to the court pursuant to the warrant of arrest in the said case on the same day after delivery of judgment and thereafter, he was sent to jail custody to serve the sentence as revealed by the order sheet of the said case. 

 4. In the Writ Petition it has been stated that the petitioner was arrested on 4-4-1998 in connection with another case i.e. Special Tribunal Case No. 80 of 1998 arising out of GR No.39 of 1998 and, as such, he was not able to be present before the Special Tribunal in connection with Special Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997. 

 5. The petitioner did not file any appeal against the judgment and order dated 27-4-1988 passed in Special Tribunal Case No.2 of 1997. He, however, filed an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 6453 of 2000 before a bench of this court which was summarily rejected and their Lordships observed, inter alia, there that the petitioner was on bail and remained in absconsion before and after passing of the impugned judgment and he was arrested in connection with another case and as the petitioner did not prefer any appeal although he had the knowledge about the impugned judgment from before. Being aggrieved and having no other alternative remedy the petitioner has filed this Writ Petition invoking Article 102 of the Constitution for an order of certiorari for quashing the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed in Special Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997 by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court and Special Tribunal No. 3, Kushtia. 

 7. Mr MA Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence was passed against the petitioner in his absence in violation of the mandatory provisions as contained in section 27(6)A of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and hence it is liable to be quashed. He further submits that the petitioner was in custody at the time when judgment was delivered and also when PWs, 3, 4 and 5 gave evidence in the case and on the other dates when hearing took place and he was not able to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses as well as make out his defence under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for no fault of his own. He further submits that since the judgment was passed in his absence when in fact he was in custody in connection with another case, therefore he was prevented from filing his appeal within the statutory period of 30 days and accordingly, the said judgment and order of conviction and sentence is liable to be set aside in this writ jurisdiction. In support of his submissions the learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied upon a number of decisions. He has firstly, quoted a passage from a decision in the case of State of UP and Md Nooh reported in AIR 1958 (SC) 73, which runs as follows: 

 8. Although we are in agreement with the principles laid down in the aforesaid decision inasmuch as this court exercising jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution has the power as well as the right to correct the error of a subordinate court such power nevertheless, will be exercised where the illegality complained of is such as to offend fair play or when the error is clearly apparent on the face of the record; it should however be added that such interference by a court exercising writ jurisdiction shall be used most sparingly and, in our opinion, in the present facts and circumstances of the case, our interference is not called for. 

 9. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has next placed the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Zahir and others reported in 45 DLR (AD) 163 where it has been held that; "if the trial is vitiated by irregularities in procedure causing prejudice to the accused that proceeding can certainly be quashed." 

 10. In that case an appeal was preferred to the Appellate Tribunal from the decision of the Special Tribunal and thereafter due to the non-availability of any other Appellate forum writ jurisdiction was invoked to set aside the conviction. 

 11. This decision will also not help the petitioner since in his case the Appellate Forum was available to him but for reason best known to him, it was not availed of. Furthermore, Criminal Miscellaneous Case under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure was also filed by the petitioner and the same was summarily rejected. Accordingly, we are of the opinion that the above mentioned decision does not apply in the present context. 

 12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner finally submits that in the case of Nesar Ahmed alias Babul vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 49 DLR (AD) 111 wherein it has been held that even though an alternative remedy was available to him he is entitled to get a relief under the writ jurisdiction. In the said case in paragraph 10 it has been stated that 

 "the presence of an alternative remedy does not debar the exercise of jurisdiction by the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution when the facts and circumstances of a particular case are such that the accused persons had no reasonable opportunity to avail of the statutory remedy under section 30 of the Special Powers Act. Whether or not the accused person had such a reasonable opportunity is a question of fact to be decided in each case upon case records and no hard and fast formula can be laid down to settle the criteria in advance." 

 13. In the instant case it appears that the petitioner was brought before the court on 27-4-1998 on the same date as judgment in the said case was delivered, albeit after delivery of judgment. Furthermore, since he was aware of the on going trial and proceeding of the case the onus was on him to make appropriate inquiry as to the progress of the trial, particularly since he obtained bail and remained in absconsion thereafter. In such circumstances it does not lie in his mouth to say that he was not aware as to when the judgment was delivered in the said case and therefore he was prevented from preferring his appeal within the statutory period of 30 days. As has been stated by their Lordships of the Appellate Division in the aforesaid case as to whether or not the accused person had a reasonable opportunity to prefer an appeal is aquestion of fact and, in our opinion; in the present case the petitioner appears to have had sufficient opportunity to prefer an appeal but he did not avail of the same for reasons best known to him.
